Guardian furniture reads "Sun 25 Oct 2026 13.31 GMT / Last modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 13.59 GMT". Retrieved by curl at 17:32 GMT.

HEADLINE: "Rayner backs Burnham call for debate on return to free movement with EU"
STANDFIRST: "Cabinet minister says PM's plea is 'pragmatism' but comments risk causing concern among some red wall MPs"
BYLINE: Rowena Mason, Whitehall editor

ANGELA RAYNER, HOUSING SECRETARY — THE CENTRAL QUOTE
The Guardian attributes this to SKY NEWS: "His remarks were supported by Rayner, the housing secretary, who told Sky News that it was 'just pragmatism'. She said: 'It's about what is the best deal for Britain and that's what we are asking the public to look at. The prime minister is clear that you can't take anything off the table when you're having a conversation.'"
Note the construction: she backs having the conversation and declines to rule anything out. She does not endorse free movement itself.

THE PRIME MINISTER'S OWN WORDS, AND THE FORUM
"The prime minister made his plea for an 'honest discussion' about free movement in an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU."
Burnham, quoted: "Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn't as difficult [as now]." / "Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."

OTHER LABOUR VOICES, ON THE RECORD
Stella Creasy, Labour MP and chair of the Labour Movement for Europe: Burnham was right that the UK was "long overdue for a grownup conversation about what EU freedom of movement actually means to our supply chains and for jobs for British citizens".
Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, is named by the Guardian as among senior cabinet ministers "in favour of reopening the discussion" and keen on a much closer EU relationship "potentially involving a return to the single market and accepting free movement as a result". This is the Guardian's characterisation, not a quote from Miliband.
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is named as "among those who have been more cautious". Her quote is retrospective, from a New Statesman event at Labour conference: rejoining the EU would not be a "simple, straightforward thing" and there were "quite hard trade-offs", such as eliminating trade friction without "some of the burdens that also brings".
Jonathan Hinder, MP for Pendle, named as a red wall MP who "recently pressed the prime minister in parliament to rule out a return to free movement". No new quote today.
Richard Walker, Labour peer and executive chair of Iceland, raised concerns ON SUNDAY, to TIMES RADIO: restarting the debate would be a "dangerous precedent" and opening the borders would not help the "one million young people that are out of work".

THE OPPOSITION, ON THE RECORD TODAY
Kemi Badenoch, Conservative leader, said reopening free movement was "another example of Burnham's foot-in-mouth syndrome". Posted on social media: "He hasn't thought this through or the implications. Most people who voted for Brexit did so because they didn't want free movement. Too many politicians have failed to understand the significance and impact of immigration on communities." / "We have had more than enough experience of what happens when politicians, including previous Conservative governments, promise control but fail to deliver it. The answer is to learn from those mistakes, not reopen free movement."
Nigel Farage, Reform UK leader, called it a "total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch", adding: "He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty."

CONTEXT CARRIED BY THE GUARDIAN
"net migration rose to a peak of about 900,000 in January 2020 under a new points-based system, up from 330,000 before the Brexit vote." [Treat this sentence with care: the Guardian pairs a peak date of January 2020 with a points-based system introduced after that date. Do not reproduce the date and the causal clause together.]
